subject: physics
pattern: The chapter normally fetches 8 to 10 marks: a 1-mark definition, a 2-mark numerical or definition, a 3-mark derivation (potential of a point charge or capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor) and often a 5-mark derivation such as energy stored in a capacitor or the effect of a dielectric slab. Numericals on series-parallel combinations and energy are very common. Examiners look for the formula, clear step-wise substitution, and correct SI units.

questions.q: Define electric potential at a point. Write its SI unit.
questions.answer: The electric potential at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive test charge from infinity to that point against the electric field: $V = \frac{W}{q_0}$. SI unit: volt (V = J C$^{-1}$).
keywords: work done per unit positive charge

questions.q: Define the capacitance of a capacitor. Write its SI unit.
questions.answer: Capacitance is the ratio of the charge given to either plate of a capacitor to the potential difference between the plates: $C = \frac{Q}{V}$. SI unit: farad (F). One farad is one coulomb per volt.
An equipotential surface is a surface on which the electric potential has the same value at every point. For a point charge, the equipotential surfaces are concentric spheres centred on the charge.

questions.q: Write any two properties of equipotential surfaces.
questions.answer: 1. No work is done in moving a test charge between two points on an equipotential surface. 2. The electric field is always perpendicular to the equipotential surface at every point. 3. Two equipotential surfaces never intersect. 4. The field is stronger where equipotential surfaces are closer together. (Any two.)

questions.q: Write the expressions for the energy stored in a charged capacitor in terms of (i) C and V, (ii) Q and C, (iii) Q and V.
questions.answer: Energy stored in a capacitor: (i) $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2$ (ii) $U = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$ (iii) $U = \frac{1}{2}QV$. The energy is stored in the electric field between the plates, with energy density $u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 E^2$.

questions.q: A 10 $\mu$F capacitor is charged by a 100 V battery. Calculate the charge on the capacitor and the energy stored in it.
questions.answer: Charge $Q = CV = 10\times10^{-6}\times100 = 1\times10^{-3}$ C. Energy $U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{1}{2}\times10\times10^{-6}\times(100)^2 = 5\times10^{-2}$ J = 0.05 J.

questions.q: Distinguish between polar and non-polar molecules with an example each.
questions.answer: Polar molecules: the centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide, so each has a permanent dipole moment (e.g. H$_2$O, HCl). Non-polar molecules: the centres of positive and negative charge coincide, so there is no permanent dipole moment (e.g. O$_2$, H$_2$, CO$_2$). In an external field, non-polar molecules acquire an induced dipole moment while polar ones tend to align along the field.

questions.q: Derive an expression for the electric potential due to a point charge at a distance r from it.
questions.answer: Let a charge +q be at O. Work done in bringing a unit positive test charge from infinity to a point P at distance r is the potential. At an intermediate distance x the field is $E = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{x^2}$ directed outward, and the external force on the test charge is $-E$. $V = -\int_{\infty}^{r}E\,dx = -\frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\int_{\infty}^{r}\frac{dx}{x^2} = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left[\frac{1}{x}\right]_{\infty}^{r}$. Hence $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{q}{r}$. V is positive for +q and negative for -q.

questions.q: Derive an expression for the electric potential at a point due to an electric dipole.
questions.answer: Dipole of charges -q at A, +q at B, separation 2a, centre O. P is at distance r from O with OP making angle $\theta$ with the dipole axis, r much larger than a. Distances: $r_1 = BP \approx r - a\cos\theta$ and $r_2 = AP \approx r + a\cos\theta$. $V = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\left(\frac{1}{r_1}-\frac{1}{r_2}\right) = \frac{q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2a\cos\theta}{r^2-a^2\cos^2\theta}$. For $r\gg a$: $V = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{p\cos\theta}{r^2}$, where $p = 2aq$. On the axial line ($\theta = 0$) $V = \frac{p}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2}$; on the equatorial line ($\theta = 90^\circ$) $V = 0$.
keywords: V = p cos theta/(4 pi eps0 r^2)

questions.q: Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with vacuum between the plates.
questions.answer: Let each plate have area A and carry charges +Q and -Q, separated by distance d (d much smaller than plate dimensions). Surface charge density $\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}$. Field between the plates (superposition of two sheets) is $E = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0} = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0 A}$ and it is zero outside. Potential difference $V = Ed = \frac{Qd}{\epsilon_0 A}$. Capacitance $C = \frac{Q}{V}$, so $C = \frac{\epsilon_0 A}{d}$. With a dielectric of constant K filling the gap, $C = \frac{K\epsilon_0 A}{d}$.

questions.q: Three capacitors of 2 $\mu$F, 3 $\mu$F and 6 $\mu$F are connected in series across a 12 V battery. Find the equivalent capacitance, the charge on each capacitor and the potential difference across each.
questions.answer: $\frac{1}{C_s} = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{6} = \frac{3+2+1}{6} = 1$, so $C_s = 1\,\mu$F. Charge on each (same in series) $Q = C_sV = 1\times10^{-6}\times12 = 12\,\mu$C. Potential differences: $V_1 = \frac{Q}{C_1} = \frac{12}{2} = 6$ V, $V_2 = \frac{12}{3} = 4$ V, $V_3 = \frac{12}{6} = 2$ V; total 12 V.

questions.q: Derive the expression for the effective capacitance of two capacitors connected in (i) series and (ii) parallel.
questions.answer: (i) Series: both capacitors carry the same charge Q, and the voltages add: $V = V_1+V_2 = \frac{Q}{C_1}+\frac{Q}{C_2}$. Since $V = \frac{Q}{C_s}$, $\frac{1}{C_s} = \frac{1}{C_1}+\frac{1}{C_2}$. (ii) Parallel: both capacitors have the same potential difference V, and the charges add: $Q = Q_1+Q_2 = C_1V+C_2V$. Since $Q = C_pV$, $C_p = C_1+C_2$. Series combination decreases the capacitance, parallel combination increases it.

questions.q: Derive an expression for the energy stored in a charged parallel plate capacitor. Hence obtain the energy density of the electric field.
questions.answer: Charging a capacitor means transferring charge from one plate to the other. When charge q is already on the plates, potential difference is $v = \frac{q}{C}$. Work done to transfer a small charge dq is $dW = v\,dq = \frac{q}{C}dq$. Total work to charge from 0 to Q: $W = \int_0^Q\frac{q}{C}dq = \frac{Q^2}{2C}$. This work is stored as potential energy: $U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}CV^2 = \frac{1}{2}QV$. Energy density: for a parallel plate capacitor $C = \frac{\epsilon_0A}{d}$ and $V = Ed$, so $U = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\epsilon_0A}{d}E^2d^2 = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2(Ad)$. Volume = Ad, hence energy per unit volume $u = \frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0E^2$.

questions.q: Derive an expression for the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor when a dielectric slab of thickness t (t < d) is introduced between the plates.
questions.answer: Plates of area A are separated by d; a slab of dielectric constant K and thickness t is inserted. Charge density on plates $\sigma = \frac{Q}{A}$. In the air gap (thickness d - t) the field is $E_0 = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$. Inside the dielectric the field is reduced to $E = \frac{E_0}{K} = \frac{\sigma}{K\epsilon_0}$. Potential difference $V = E_0(d-t)+Et = \frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\left[(d-t)+\frac{t}{K}\right] = \frac{Q}{\epsilon_0A}\left[d-t+\frac{t}{K}\right]$. Capacitance $C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{\epsilon_0A}{d-t\left(1-\frac{1}{K}\right)}$. If the slab fills the gap (t = d), $C = \frac{K\epsilon_0A}{d}$. For a conducting slab, $K\to\infty$ and $C = \frac{\epsilon_0A}{d-t}$.
keywords: field reduced to E0/K in dielectric
